result:
At the edge of every city there is a place where the streetlights become uncertain.

The sidewalks thin out. Buildings lose their names. A grocery store sits alone beside a six-lane road, illuminated all night for reasons nobody can fully explain. Behind it, weeds climb through a chain-link fence, and beyond the fence there may be a field, a warehouse, a drainage canal, or simply darkness.

These places are easy to ignore because they do not announce themselves as destinations. No one writes postcards from the parking lot of a closed furniture outlet. No one says, “Meet me by the empty bus stop beside the overpass; it’s beautiful there.” Yet they contain a strange kind of honesty.

In the center of a city, everything has been arranged to persuade you. Windows invite you in. Signs tell you what to want. Parks have benches placed at careful angles, and cafés play music selected to make time feel pleasantly expensive. But at the outskirts, the city seems to run out of sentences. It stops trying to explain itself.

There, you can see the machinery underneath: utility poles leaning slightly in the wind, service roads patched with asphalt of several different shades, gulls circling a landfill, distant apartment towers glowing like computer screens. You can see how much effort is required just to keep ordinary life moving—electricity, deliveries, buses, storm drains, warehouses, late-night workers in reflective jackets.

Maybe that is why such places feel lonely. They reveal that the world continues without applause.

Still, there is comfort in that. A lone convenience store at midnight can feel more welcoming than a grand hall full of strangers. The humming refrigerators, the tired cashier, the rotating rack of snacks—all of it says: you are allowed to exist here for a moment. You may buy a bottle of water. You may stand beneath the fluorescent lights. You may be between places.

Most of life is probably spent between places.

We imagine ourselves moving from beginning to ending, from ambition to achievement, from one clear chapter to another. But the truth is that we spend years in the parking lots of the soul: waiting, regrouping, taking wrong turns, checking our directions, watching rain collect in the cracks.

Perhaps that is not wasted time. Perhaps the in-between is where we learn to notice things: the small warmth of a paper cup, the sound of tires on wet pavement, the fact that someone somewhere has left a light on.
